questions.question: Statements: Only a few books are pens. All pens are pencils. No pencil is an eraser. Conclusions: I. Some books are pencils. II. No pen is an eraser. III. All books can never be pencils. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.explanation: Conclusions I and II are definite, while Conclusion III is incorrect as all books can be pencils.
Conclusion III does not follow as all books can be pencils.
Conclusion III does not follow, and Conclusion I is also correct.

options.text: All I, II and III follow.
options.explanation: Conclusion III does not follow.

questions.explanation: 'Only a few books are pens' implies two things: (1) Some books are pens, and (2) Some books are not pens. I. From 'Only a few books are pens' (which means Some books are pens) and 'All pens are pencils': Since all pens are pencils, and some books are pens, it definitely follows that 'Some books are pencils'. II. From 'All pens are pencils' and 'No pencil is an eraser': If no pencil is an eraser, and all pens are pencils, then definitely 'No pen is an eraser'. III. 'All books can never be pencils': This means 'All books being pencils is not a possibility'. From 'Only a few books are pens' (meaning Some books are not pens) and 'All pens are pencils', it is still possible for ALL books to be pencils. The 'some books are not pens' part doesn't restrict all books from being pencils, as long as the pens themselves are also pencils. For example, if Books = {B1, B2, B3}, Pens = {B1}, Pencils = {B1, B2, B3}. Here, only a few books are pens (B1), and all books are pencils. So, 'All books can never be pencils' is false; it *is* a possibility.
questions.hint: Analyze the implications of 'Only a few' and the possibility of overlapping sets.
